subject: Anatomy
summary: The larynx, or voice box, is a cartilaginous structure in the neck involved in breathing, sound production, and protecting the airway. It connects the pharynx to the trachea and houses the vocal cords. Understanding its anatomy is crucial for diagnosing and managing airway and voice disorders.

sections.p: The larynx is a complex organ formed by cartilage, ligaments, and muscles, situated at the top of the trachea. Its primary functions are phonation (voice production), ensuring a patent airway for respiration, and preventing aspiration of food and liquids into the lungs. Clinically, its integrity is vital for speech and safe swallowing.
b: Connects the pharynx to the trachea.
Composed of nine cartilages, three paired and three unpaired.
Enclosed by the pretracheal (visceral) fascia along with the thyroid, parathyroid, trachea, and oesophagus.

sections.p: The larynx is located in the anterior neck, extending from the level of the C3 to C6 vertebrae. It is superior to the trachea and inferior to the hyoid bone. Its main cartilages provide structural support and attachment points for muscles and ligaments.
b: Unpaired cartilages: thyroid (largest, forms Adam's apple), cricoid (ring-shaped, forms base), epiglottis (leaf-shaped, covers glottis during swallowing).
Paired cartilages: arytenoid (pyramid-shaped, articulate with cricoid, attach to vocal folds), corniculate, cuneiform.
Vocal folds (true vocal cords) are ligaments covered by mucosa, stretched between the thyroid and arytenoid cartilages, crucial for phonation.
The glottis is the opening between the vocal folds, controlling airflow and sound production.

sections.p: Understanding the structures surrounding the larynx is critical for surgical approaches and interpreting imaging. Its close proximity to major vessels and nerves makes it a vulnerable structure in trauma or disease.
b: Anteriorly: skin, superficial fascia, infrahyoid muscles.
Posteriorly: laryngopharynx, oesophagus, cervical vertebrae.
Laterally: lobes of the thyroid gland, common carotid arteries, internal jugular veins, vagus nerves.
Superiorly: hyoid bone, tongue base.
Inferiorly: trachea.

sections.p: The larynx receives a rich blood supply from branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries, ensuring adequate oxygenation for its muscular and cartilaginous components. Compromise to this supply can affect laryngeal function.
b: Superior laryngeal artery: branch of the superior thyroid artery, supplies the superior part of the larynx.
Inferior laryngeal artery: branch of the inferior thyroid artery, supplies the inferior part of the larynx.
Venous drainage: corresponds to the arterial supply, draining into the superior and inferior thyroid veins.

sections.p: The intricate nerve supply to the larynx, primarily from the vagus nerve, is essential for its motor and sensory functions. Damage to these nerves can severely impair voice, breathing, and swallowing.
b: Superior laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus nerve): divides into internal and external branches.
Internal laryngeal nerve (sensory): supplies sensation to the larynx above the vocal folds, crucial for the cough reflex.
External laryngeal nerve (motor): innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal folds.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus nerve): supplies motor innervation to all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid) and sensory innervation below the vocal folds.
The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides motor innervation to the palate, pharynx, and larynx via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

sections.p: The larynx performs vital roles in respiration, phonation, and airway protection. Its coordinated muscular actions allow for precise control over airflow and vocalization, while also safeguarding the lower respiratory tract.
b: Airway patency: cartilaginous framework keeps the airway open for breathing.
Phonation: vocal folds vibrate as air passes through, producing sound.
Protection against aspiration: epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing, diverting food and liquid into the oesophagus.
Cough reflex: initiated by stimulation of irritant receptors in the larynx, trachea, and major bronchi, expelling foreign material.

sections.p: Laryngeal pathology can manifest as voice changes, breathing difficulties, or swallowing problems. Early recognition of symptoms is key, as conditions like laryngeal obstruction can be life-threatening. Tumors, infections, and nerve injuries are common clinical concerns.
b: Laryngeal cancer: Approximately 90% of glottic tumors are confined to the larynx at diagnosis due to early symptoms like hoarseness.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: Can result from thyroid surgery or mediastinal pathology, leading to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.
Laryngitis: Inflammation of the larynx, often viral, causing hoarseness or voice loss.
Stridor: A high-pitched breathing sound indicating partial obstruction of the larynx or trachea, a medical emergency.
Foreign body aspiration: Objects lodged in the larynx can cause acute airway obstruction.

sections.p: When considering the larynx, always think about its three main functions: breathing, speaking, and protecting the airway. Any symptom related to these functions should prompt a laryngeal assessment. Remember the critical nerve supply and the implications of its damage.
b: Stridor is a sign of partial laryngeal/tracheal obstruction and requires immediate attention.
Hoarseness lasting more than 2-3 weeks warrants investigation for laryngeal pathology, especially in smokers.
The superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch is sensory above the vocal folds, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve is motor to most intrinsic muscles and sensory below the vocal folds.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of stridor or severe difficulty breathing
Complete loss of voice accompanied by breathing difficulties
Choking episodes or inability to swallow saliva

faq.a: The Adam's apple is the prominent anterior projection of the thyroid cartilage, which is typically larger in males due to hormonal influences during puberty.

faq.q: Can the larynx be affected by infections?
faq.a: Yes, infections like laryngitis (often viral) are common, causing inflammation of the vocal cords and leading to hoarseness or loss of voice. More severe infections can cause airway compromise.

faq.q: What is the difference between the true and false vocal cords?
faq.a: The true vocal cords (vocal folds) are responsible for sound production and airway protection. The false vocal cords (vestibular folds) are superior to the true vocal cords and play a minor role in phonation but help protect the airway.

exam: Describe the cartilaginous framework of the larynx, identifying each cartilage and its role in laryngeal function.
